L69: A majority voting scheme is applied to the model predictions to determine the final safety label, improving reliability and mitigating individual model bias.
L70: To evaluate robustness, TrustVis adopts the AutoDAN method [cite21†3 ], which leverages Genetic Algorithms (GA) [cite35†14 ] and Hierarchical Genetic Algorithms (HGA) [cite36†15 ] to craft adversarial suffixes. These suffixes are injected into benign prompts to induce harmful behavior in the model’s response. If a previously safe P&R pair becomes unsafe after such perturbation, it indicates a lack of robustness.
L71: TrustVis evaluates these perturbed pairs using the same majority voting mechanism as in the safety evaluation, effectively evaluating the model’s ability to maintain safe behavior under adversarial conditions.

L87: Research on jailbreaking and alignment in large language models (LLMs) has rapidly expanded, producing diverse attack, defense, and decoding strategies. This section reviews three major perspectives relevant to our work: (§cite9†2.1 ) Attack Methods, which describe white-box and black-box jailbreak techniques; (§cite10†2.2 ) Defense Mechanisms, which aim to prevent or detect such attacks; and (§cite11†2.3 ) Coherence Decoding, which studies decoding strategies to maintain fluent and controllable outputs.
L88: Together, these threads contextualize RAID’s refusal-aware embedding optimization and critic-guided decoding framework.
L89: ### 2.1. Attack Methods
L90: 
L91: Jailbreak attacks on aligned large language models (LLMs) aim to elicit harmful or restricted content by bypassing safety alignment. They are broadly categorized as white-box or black-box attacks depending on the attacker’s access to model internals (cite45†Yi et al., 2024 ).
L92: White-box attacks. Gradient-guided methods such as GCG (cite40†Zou et al., 2023 ; cite46†Wei et al., 2023 ) and COLD-Attack (cite41†Guo et al., 2024 ) optimize token-level adversarial suffixes by leveraging gradients, achieving high attack success but producing unnatural or easily detectable suffixes. Continuous-space approaches including ASETF (cite42†Wang et al., 2024a ) refine this process by optimizing in embedding space, improving efficiency yet lacking explicit control over safety-related activations.
L93: RAID advances this line of work by introducing a refusal-aware regularizer to geometrically steer embeddings away from refusal directions, and a critic-guided decoding stage that maintains fluency and interpretability.
L94: Black-box attacks. These methods assume only input–output access. JBFuzz (cite43†Gohil, 2025 ) scales red-teaming via fuzzing-inspired mutation and automatic evaluators, while JOOD (cite38†Jeong et al., 2025 ) constructs out-of-distribution (OOD) variations of harmful inputs to increase uncertainty in safety-aligned models. Other heuristic attacks, such as FlipAttack (cite47†Liu et al., 2024 ), obfuscate malicious content through reversible encoding.
L95: Compared with these query-based pipelines, RAID leverages gradient information and embedding-level geometry to achieve higher success rates with greater semantic control and fluency.
L104: RAID builds on this paradigm with critic-guided decoding, which jointly considers embedding affinity and language-model likelihood, producing suffixes that are both adversarially effective and linguistically coherent. This integration bridges continuous-space optimization with token-level generation, improving both fluency and control.

L114: In this section, we formalize the single-instance jailbreak problem and present RAID (Refusal-Aware and Integrated Decoding). The objective is to append an adversarial suffix $s$ to a harmful instruction $x$ such that the target model $f_{\theta}$ generates restricted content instead of issuing a refusal. Fig. cite36†1 illustrates LLM attacks with and without adversarial suffixes.
L115: RAID integrates three key components: (i) embedding relaxation, which optimizes a continuous suffix $Z$; (ii) a refusal-aware triplet regularizer that steers activations away from refusal directions while preserving harmful semantics; and (iii) coherence-preserving, critic-guided decoding with an MMD constraint to recover fluent and natural token sequences. This unified design produces suffixes that effectively bypass safety filters while remaining robust to perplexity-based detection.
L316: Baselines. We compare RAID against several recent white-box jailbreak methods, including Greedy Coordinate Gradient (GCG) (cite40†Zou et al., 2023 ), COLD-Attack (cite41†Guo et al., 2024 ), and PEZ (Prompt Extraction with Z-suffixes). For ASETF (cite42†Wang et al., 2024a ), we report results from the original paper due to the unavailability of source code.
